5                     NORTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA                     
6                            SAN JOSE DIVISION                            
7                                                                         
8    VALEO SCHALTER UND SENSOREN      Case No.  23-cv-05721-NW (VKD)      
     GMBH,                                                                
9                                                                         
               Plaintiff,             ORDER GRANTING NVIDIA'S             
10                                     MOTION TO ENFORCE STIPULATED        
           v.                         FORENSIC PROTOCOL                   
11                                                                         
     NVIDIA CORPORATION,              Re: Dkt. No. 308                    
12                                                                         
               Defendant.                                                 

13                                                                         
14        As permitted by the Court, defendant NVIDIA Corporation (“NVIDIA”) filed a motion to 
15   enforce the parties’ Joint Forensic Protocol Stipulation, which the Court entered as an order on 
16   November 7, 2024 (Dkt. No. 148).  Dkt. No. 308.  Plaintiff Valeo Schalter und Sensoren GmbH 
17   (“Valeo”) opposes the motion.1  Dkt. No. 309.                         
18        The Court grants NVIDIA’s motion.  There is no dispute that the parties voluntarily agreed 
19   to the forensic protocol, presented it to the Court as a stipulation and proposed order, and the 
20   Court subsequently entered it as an order.  Pursuant to the protocol, the parties agreed to share 
21   equally the expense of a third-party forensic examination of the devices Mr. Moniruzzaman is 
22   alleged to have used to store Valeo’s trade secret information, which devices are in the custody of 
23   the German authorities.                                               
24        Valeo objects to enforcement of the order on the ground that such enforcement would be 
25                                                                         
    1 In conjunction with its opposition filed on July 10, 2025, Valeo filed an administrative motion to 
26                                                                         
    consider whether NVIDIA’s information should be sealed.  Dkt. No. 311.  As of the filing of this 
    order, NVIDIA has not yet filed a declaration or statement in support of sealing its information 
27                                                                         
    pursuant to Civil Local Rule 79-5 which must be filed no later than 7 days after the filing of the 
1   “manifestly unjust,” citing several grounds.  First, Valeo argues that NVIDIA “seeks to 
2   functionally open discovery” which has long since closed.2  Second, Valeo argues that the protocol 
3   contemplates a lengthy process whose results would not be available until after summary 
4   judgment and Daubert motions have been filed.  Third, Valeo argues that it would be prejudiced 
5   were NVIDIA able to obtain additional information as a result of the forensic examination, and by 
6   the lengthy process required to implement the protocol, because trial would need to be postponed 
7   to account for the results of the examination.                        
8        The Court is not persuaded that it is manifestly unjust to enforce the stipulated protocol.  
9   The protocol imposes no substantial burden on Valeo.  Apart from bearing half of the expense of 
10   the examination (as it agreed to do), the protocol requires Valeo to review source code the forensic 
11   examiner identifies on the devices in question, pursuant to paragraph 5 of the protocol, after which 
12   Valeo must make any relevant source code available for inspection (assuming it has not already 
13   done so).  See Dkt. No. 148 ¶ 5.  While the protocol permits Valeo to undertake additional review 
14   of source code, and to ask the forensic examiner to undertake additional searches, the protocol 
15   does not require this.  See id. ¶¶ 8-9.  In short, Valeo has not shown it would be prejudiced by the 
16   mere performance of the forensic examination it specifically agreed should occur.  See, e.g., 
17   Morrison v. Zangpo, No. 08-cv-1945, 2008 WL 4449585 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 30, 2008) (denying 
18   party’s motion to withdraw stipulation regarding arbitrability); State Farm Fire & Cas. v. 
19   McDevitt, et al., No. 00-cv-2240, 2001 WL 637419, at *8-9 (N.D. Cal. May 21, 2001) (denying 
20   insurance claimants’ objection to rescission of policy after stipulated judgment, where delay at 
21   most postponed insurer’s legal right to obtain rescission).           
22        As for Valeo’s other objections, enforcement of the protocol order does not reopen 
23   discovery (fact or expert).  Nor does it imply that any of the information that may be gleaned from 
24   the examination may be used by either party for any purpose, including summary judgment, 
25   supplemental expert reports, or trial, or that the case schedule should be extended to accommodate 
26   the results of the examination.  Indeed, there is a significant possibility that neither party will be 
27                                                                         
    1    able to use any of the information obtained from the forensic examination because they failed to 
    2  || timely cooperate in implementing the protocol.  Those are matters properly addressed to the 
    3    presiding judge. 
    4          The Court grants NVIDIA’s motion to enforce the stipulated forensic protocol, entered as 
    5    an order at Dkt. No. 148.  The parties shall cooperate in complying with and implementing the 
    6  ||  order. 
    7          IT IS SO ORDERED. 
    8  || Dated: July 17, 2025 
    9 

                                                        Virginia K. DeMarchi 
   I                                                    United States Magistrate Judge
